name: Dead Internet theory
title: Is Anyone Actually There? Checking the Dead Internet Claim
claims: Dead internet theory asserts the internet consists primarily of bot activity and automated content shaped by algorithmic curation | 1
Original conception was a conspiracy theory of coordinated effort to control the population | 1
Magazine account: theory says internet died sometime in 2016, populated mostly by bots, AIs and deepfakes | 2
Theory spread because it captures the feeling of being online: inorganic fakery and automation | 2
First post thought to have originated on image board Wizardchan | 1
In 2021 a forum post titled "Dead Internet Theory: Most Of The Internet Is Fake" was published on Agora Road's Macintosh Cafe, building on earlier posts from the same board and Wizardchan | 1
Theory spread via YouTube, Reddit and Twitter | 1
September 2021 Atlantic article "Maybe You Missed It, but the Internet 'Died' Five Years Ago", widely cited | 1
Original post described bots displacing humans as the "setup" and the US government as the "thesis" | 1
Quoted thesis: "The U.S. government is engaging in an artificial intelligence-powered gaslighting of the entire world population." | 1
Original post cited 2018 New York magazine article "How Much of the Internet Is Fake? Turns Out, a Lot of It, Actually" | 1
2016 Imperva report examined over 16.7 billion visits to 100,000 randomly selected domains and found 52% of web traffic was automated | 1
Imperva 2023 report: 49.6% automated, a 2% rise from 2022, partly attributed to AI models scraping the web for training content | 1
Fortune reported that as of 2026 more than half of website requests were generated by bots | 1

In 2022 a Copenhagen Institute for Futures Studies researcher said that if GPT-3 "gets loose" the Internet would be completely unrecognizable, and predicted 99% to 99.9% of content AI-generated by 2025 to 2030 | 1
Those predictions have been used as evidence for the theory | 1
Late 2022 release of ChatGPT led journalists to call the theory potentially more realistic than before | 1
Before ChatGPT the theory emphasized government organizations, corporations and tech-literate individuals; ChatGPT gave average users access to LLMs | 1
Magazine writer said the theory got a shot in the arm from ChatGPT's release | 2
Writer described an "Internet of Bullshit": avalanche of passably well-written content with nothing beneath the surface | 2
ChatGPT, asked about its influence, said its stories would lack depth, emotion and humanity | 2
In 2024 AI-generated images ("AI slop") including flight attendants, children next to artwork and "Shrimp Jesus" went viral on Facebook | 1
Many posts had hundreds or thousands of comments saying "Amen" | 1
Images cited as example of the Internet beginning to feel "dead" | 1
An academic article used Shrimp Jesus as a symbol of the shift, quote about "fatal system", "exponential metastasis" | 1
In 2020 Twitter accounts posted tweets starting "I hate texting" with tens of thousands of likes, many suspected from bots; proponents use it as an example | 1
January 2025 Meta announced plans for AI-powered autonomous accounts; Meta VP quote about bios, profile pictures and generating content; accounts quickly removed | 1
Facebook offers AI responses to group posts when @MetaAI is tagged or when a question gets no reply within an hour | 1
Reddit once allowed free API access, which allowed moderation apps and training AI; in 2023 it moved to charge for data | 1
LLMs increasingly used on Reddit by users and bot accounts | 1
A computer scientist said training next-generation AI on previous generations' content could cause content to suffer | 1
A professor compared AI content flooding Reddit to the dead internet theory | 1
September 2025 OpenAI's CEO posted on Twitter/X that he never took the theory that seriously but there seemed to be a lot of LLM-run accounts; post went viral | 1
In 2024 Google reported results inundated with sites that "feel like they were created for search engines instead of people" | 1
Google spokesperson told Gizmodo generative AI had a role and could displace more valuable human-made content | 1
Bots using LLMs could create "self-replicating prompts" resulting in loops only human users could disrupt | 1
Proponents claim Google censors the web, filters what is indexed, calls Google a Potemkin village; link rot is cited | 1
Link rot is when content becomes unavailable and links to it break | 1
Second half of theory claims government, corporations or other actors intentionally limit users to curated, AI-generated content | 1
2025 book chapter described "weak" version (elites using bots to shape discourse) and "strong" version (society collapsed, entity such as aliens or advanced AI keeps people online to disguise it) | 1

2026 article described a "leaner" theory "stripped of paranoia, prejudice, politics and polemic", core being algorithmically generated content, generative AI byproducts, difficulty distinguishing from human content, and resulting mistrust and misinformation | 1
Author lamented conspiracy theorists make implausible claims but argued core criticisms should not be dismissed | 1
One source uses the term "Dead Internet" for spaces hosting generative content, dropping "theory" | 1
Commentators see the theory as having some truth or as a realistic prediction of the Internet's future | 1

sources.title: Did A.I. just become a better storyteller than you?
